summary: Young children (around ages 5-6) learn to MEASURE elapsed time using tools — sand timers, stopwatches, counting seconds — to time real activities and record results in simple units ('about 2 minutes'). The core skill is procedural and embodied: start the tool exactly as the event begins, stop it exactly as it ends, then read off the duration. The conceptual underpinnings are that duration is how long something lasts from start to finish, measured with a tool rather than judged by how fast, effortful or busy the activity felt, and that 1 minute = 60 seconds, which is a genuine conceptual step because 60 is not a base-ten grouping.
misconceptions: Judges duration by speed or by how much happened, not elapsed time (carried from comparing durations)
Starts or stops the tool out of step with the event
Reads the number currently showing as the duration, ignoring where timing started
Thinks 'a minute' and '60 seconds' are different amounts

activities.title: Time a real activity with start and stop aligned to the event
steps: Pick a short, real activity to time (e.g. writing your name five times, tidying a small tray, building a block tower).

Choose the right tool: for an open-ended duration use a stopwatch or a seconds count/large seconds display; a fixed one-minute sand timer is best for checking whether something takes about a minute or comparing against its known span.
Hold the visible timing tool ready.
Count '3-2-1 start' and start the tool at the exact moment the activity begins.
Stop the tool the instant the activity finishes (on the last action).
Read off and say the duration in simple terms, e.g. 'about half a minute', 'about 40 seconds', 'a bit more than a minute'.
Repeat with a second activity and compare which took longer.
activities.insight: 'How long' is a quantity you can capture with a tool by aligning start and stop with the event, not a feeling guessed from how fast or how effortful the activity was.

activities.title: Build 1 minute = 60 seconds by counting a one-minute timer
steps: Turn over a one-minute sand timer and count the seconds aloud (or follow a seconds display) until the sand runs out.

Notice that the count reaches about 60 as the minute ends, provided each number is paced to one second (e.g. by following a seconds display); young children counting freely often go faster and reach a higher number.
Say the relationship: 'one minute is the same as 60 seconds.'
Check with a second tool: 'If we used the stopwatch instead, would it agree?'
activities.insight: A minute and 60 seconds are the same amount of time, not two different amounts — the 60-grouping is something you can experience by counting it out.

activities.title: Compare two durations and read a growing span, not the end number
steps: Time two different activities and record each duration ('about 20 seconds', 'about a minute').
Represent each duration as a length — e.g. a bar that grows FROM the start, or line up the two timings side by side.
Decide which activity took longer by comparing the lengths.
If using a stopwatch, note or zero the start first, so the duration is the span covered, not whichever number happens to show at the end.
activities.insight: Duration is the amount of time that elapsed between start and stop — represented as a length that grows from the start — not simply the number currently displayed.

checkQuestion: Set a real timing task and WATCH (don't ask the child to explain the procedure): 'Here is a one-minute sand timer and a stopwatch. Time how long it takes you to write your name five times — start the timer as you begin and stop it as you finish, then tell me about how long it took. Then turn the one-minute sand timer over and count how many seconds go by until the sand runs out.'
checkAnswer: Starts the tool as the activity begins and stops it as it ends; reads and reports the duration in sensible units ('about half a minute', 'about 40 seconds'); counts roughly to 60 as the one-minute timer empties, showing a beginning grasp that 1 minute = 60 seconds.
